description: Surviving on Mars requires quick, tactical navigation. The Interplanetary Survival Map is a conceptual framework designed to translate planetary data into surface survival tools. Using NASA elevation, radiation, and ice datasets, our concept maps landing risks, steep terrain, and shelter options like lava tubes. Designed with a clear, functional interface, it aims to guide safe rover paths and habitat placement, bridging complex planetary science with human survival on the Red Planet.
summary:
CARTEX (Cartographic Tactical Exploration System) is an integrated, browser-based mission planning and real-time navigation platform designed for human Mars surface exploration. Built in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, CARTEX layers multiple NASA data sources — including MOLA topography, Viking MDIM 2.1 imagery, THEMIS thermal maps, Curiosity rover telemetry, and live space weather feeds — into a unified, interactive interface.

The platform features a 3D rover simulation with EVA astronaut companion, 2D/3D surface mapping via OpenLayers and Three.js, scientific target prioritization, atmospheric and radiation monitoring, crew biometrics tracking, and an AI-assisted mission planning assistant. Data from JPL Mars Trek, NASA PDS, and MAAS2 API are combined to give astronauts and mission controllers a hyperlocalized, layered view of their target terrain.

CARTEX addresses the challenge's core requirement: providing a tool that is actionable at the individual spacewalk level — not just regional or global. By fusing geology, slope traversability, radiation risk, thermal data, and real rover imagery into one decision-ready interface, CARTEX empowers the first human Mars explorers to plan safer routes, conduct richer science, and respond to surface hazards in real time.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

CARTEX (Cartographic Tactical Exploration System) is a multi-panel, browser-based mission planning and real-time navigation platform for human Mars surface exploration. It integrates layered NASA datasets into a single, decision-ready interface. The platform features: a live 2D surface map (OpenLayers) with togglable MOLA topography, THEMIS thermal, Viking MDIM 2.1 basemap, and slope overlays; a 3D rover simulation (Three.js) with real terrain height-mapping, a third-person EVA astronaut companion with animated walking motion, dig trench excavation mechanics, and multiple camera modes (Mastcam POV, HazCam Wheel, 3rd Chase, EVA Walk); an AI mission planning assistant; crew biometrics and suit telemetry monitoring; atmospheric and radiation dashboards using live NASA API data; and a full mission report and dossier export system.

NASA Data Sources Used

  • MOLA (Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter) — topographic elevation data
  • Viking MDIM 2.1 — global Mars texture basemap
  • THEMIS (Thermal Emission Imaging System) — thermal infrared overlays
  • NASA MAAS2 API — real-time Mars weather (temperature, pressure, wind)
  • NASA PDS / Curiosity rover telemetry — scientific instrument data (PIXL, SHERLOC, SuperCam, Mastcam-Z, MOXIE)
  • InSight seismic data — subsurface reference
  • NASA JPL Mars Trek layers — geologic and spectral data

Benefits & Intended Impact

CARTEX bridges the gap between global Mars mapping tools (like JPL Mars Trek) and the hyperlocalized, real-time needs of a human astronaut on a surface excursion. It prioritizes astronaut safety by surfacing radiation risk, slope traversability alerts, and suit pressure warnings in real time. The layered data approach means a crew member or mission controller can instantly understand geology, thermal conditions, terrain obstacles, and atmospheric hazards at their specific location — not just at a planetary scale.

Tools, Languages & Technologies

  • Frontend: Next.js 16.4.3 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript 5
  • 3D Rendering: Three.js 0.187
  • 2D Mapping: OpenLayers 10
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS v4
  • APIs: NASA MAAS2, NASA PDS, MOLA/THEMIS data endpoints
  • AI Assistant: Integrated natural language mission planner
  • Platform: Web-based, runs in any modern browser, no installation required

Creativity & Team Considerations

We chose a heads-up-display (HUD) design language inspired by real NASA mission control interfaces and sci-fi EVA suit visors — making data feel immersive and mission-ready rather than academic. We prioritized safety-first design: every panel surfaces risk data prominently. The 3D astronaut companion in EVA_WALK mode lets users visualize the human scale of exploration against the Martian terrain. The team considered mobility constraints of a suited astronaut, communication latency (one-way light lag displayed live), buddy separation rules, and metabolic workload — factors a real Mars crew would face.
